hints: Notice the conditions, hot concentrated ethanolic NaOH points to elimination to form an alkene, not substitution to form an alcohol.
Draw out $(CH_3)_2CBrCH_2CH_2CH_3$ and look for the different beta-carbons next to C2 that have hydrogens to lose.
Remove H from the C1 methyl groups for one alkene, and from the C3 $CH_2$ group for the other, then name both double bond positions.
walkthrough:
**Spot the reaction type**

Great start, the conditions tell you everything. Hot, concentrated, ethanolic NaOH means elimination of $HBr$ to give alkenes.

$$\text{halogenoalkane} + \text{NaOH (ethanolic, hot)} \rightarrow \text{alkene} + \text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Draw the starting structure**

Let's make it visual. 2-bromo-2-methylpentane is a tertiary bromoalkane.

$$\text{CH}_3-\text{C(Br)(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$$
The C-Br is on C2. The carbons next to it with H atoms are C1 and C3.

**Find the two elimination routes**

Elimination removes Br from C2 plus H from a neighbour. There are two different neighbours here.

Route 1, H from C1 (a methyl group): $$\text{CH}_2=\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$$
Route 2, H from C3 ($CH_2$ group): $$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$$

**Name the products and choose**

Route 1 gives the terminal alkene, 2-methylpent-1-ene. Route 2 gives the more substituted internal alkene, 2-methylpent-2-ene. Both form as a mixture, so you expect two products.

options.A: Not complete. 2-methylpent-1-ene does form by losing H from a C1 methyl group, but it is not the only product because H can also be lost from C3.
options.B: Correct and well done. Loss of H from C1 gives 2-methylpent-1-ene and loss of H from C3 gives 2-methylpent-2-ene, so both alkenes are produced by elimination.
options.C: Not complete. 2-methylpent-2-ene is the major, more substituted product from losing H at C3, but the minor product from C1 still forms, so it is not formed only.
options.D: Incorrect. 4-methylpent-2-ene has the methyl branch in the wrong place and cannot form here without rearranging the carbon skeleton, which does not happen in simple elimination.
